Exit code 1
# The Demo {#sec-the-demo}

The third answer wasn't a sentence.

Hedda asked how the book was, in the last four minutes, the way she always had.
I said, "Can I show you?"

She looked at me a moment.
Then she turned her monitor toward me.

I had rehearsed it for a week.
Every evening I sat at the kitchen table, ran the tool on Full Stop, and talked to nobody about what it found, with a timer on my phone set to four minutes.
The first night it took nine.
By the end of the week it took four, and I no longer needed the notes I had written for it, which I brought anyway.

It found the same thing every night.
That was what I liked about it.
The shop in chapter four, the shop in chapter nine, and the one claim they could not both be making.
I knew where it would appear on the screen and how long it would take to get there, and I had a sentence ready for when it did.

I plugged my laptop into Hedda's monitor and ran it.

The tool reads the list of claims first, then the chapters.
For each claim it prints every sentence that makes it, with the chapter and the line.
Most of them are green, and they go by too fast to read.

It found the two shops in under a second.

There they were, near the bottom: one claim, and under it two sentences, one from chapter four and one from chapter nine, saying different things about who made the dash fashionable.
The claim was orange.
I had expected that.
I had expected it seven nights running.

Under the shops were three more.

I had not expected those.

The night before, I had fixed something.
Chapter three had a date in it that chapter eight had quietly moved by a decade, and it had been on the tool's list since the first Sunday.
I had finally made chapter three agree with chapter eight.
It took one sentence.
I went to bed pleased.

I had not run the tool after.
I had rehearsed the demo.
I had not rehearsed the book.

The date was not only in chapter three.
It was in three other sentences, in three other chapters, which had agreed with chapter three for years and had not been told.
On Hedda's monitor the date sat at the top, once, as a claim, and under it were the four places it lived, three of them in red, disagreeing with a sentence I had written the night before.

I had a sentence ready for the two shops.
I had nothing ready for this.

So I showed her.
I pointed at the claim, and at each sentence under it, and said which chapter it came from and what it was about.
It took longer than four minutes.
It was easier than any answer I had given her in three years.
I did not have to describe the problem.
It was on her monitor, in four lines.

Hedda read it.
Not the summary at the bottom: the sentences.

Somewhere around the third of the four lines, the half hour ended.
Hedda has a hard stop at the half hour.
She watched all of it.

She asked one question, in the middle.
She pointed at the two shops and asked what the orange meant.

"Contradicts, but I like it," I said.

She wrote that down.
I don't know where.

When the tool had finished, the screen held four contradictions and a count at the bottom that said so.
Hedda sat back and looked at it for a while.

Then she asked whether the book was done.

"No," I said.

I heard myself say it.
It was the first time the true answer to her question was shorter than the demo.

She nodded, and wrote something down, and we both stood up, nine minutes late.

Hedda's running document is shared with me.
I open it more often than I would like to say.
It changed again that week.

```text
Paint a book cover. Portrait, 1600 by 2560 pixels.

The scene: a kitchen table late in the evening, seen from a little above.
On the left side of the table sits a tall stack of manuscript pages,
squared up and tied with string, a pencil lying across the top. It has
not been touched in a long time; it is tidy and slightly sad. On the
right side, where someone has actually been working, is cheerful
disorder: a shoebox full of index cards, a few cards fanned out of it, an
open laptop whose screen shows only plain rows of gray lines, a mug, and
a single printed sheet with one line circled. Everything on the right is
turned slightly away from the stack, as if the work wandered off from it
on purpose. No people and no hands; the person has just stepped out.

The mood is dry and quietly funny, not wistful: a well-organized escape
from a job that was never finished. Restrained and observational, the way
a good cartoon is restrained.

Style: a painting, not a photograph and not a diagram. Ink and gray wash
on warm off-white paper, loose but precise, with plenty of untouched
paper showing.

Color: black ink and grays only, on the paper's own off-white. Exactly
one spot of color in the whole image: the circle drawn around the line on
the printed sheet, in orange (#E8740C). No other color anywhere: no
blue, no green, no brown, no warm-tinted grays.

No text of any kind. No letters, words, numbers, logos, signatures or
legible writing anywhere, including on the pages, the cards and the
screen: every page, card and screen shows only abstract gray lines.

Leave the top third of the image calm and nearly empty (open wall or
plain paper tone) and a quiet strip along the bottom, so a title and an
author's name can be set over them later. Keep the table and objects in
the middle.
```
